What functions do you think bearings serve, and why can't rotating shafts simply rest directly in their housings? ::: ## Introduction to Bearings {#sec-bearings-intro} Bearings are machine elements that **constrain relative motion** and **reduce friction** between moving parts. They are fundamental to virtually every rotating machine—from tiny precision instruments to massive industrial equipment. Bearings serve three primary functions: 1. **Support loads** (radial and/or thrust) 2. **Reduce friction** between moving surfaces 3. **Guide motion** with precision and repeatability --- ### Classification of Bearings {-} Bearings are broadly classified into two main categories: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Classification of bearing types.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/bearing-classification-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- ## Ball Bearings {-} Ball bearings are the most common type of rolling element bearing. They use spherical balls as the rolling elements, held between an inner race and an outer race. ### Anatomy of a Ball Bearing {-} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cross-section of a deep groove ball bearing showing main components.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/ball-bearing-anatomy-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: **Key Components:** | Component | Function | |:----------|:---------| | **Inner Race** | Mounted on the shaft; rotates with the shaft | | **Outer Race** | Mounted in the housing; typically stationary | | **Rolling Elements** | Balls that roll between races, carrying the load | | **Cage (Retainer)** | Separates and guides the balls to prevent contact | | **Seals/Shields** | Keep lubricant in and contaminants out | --- ### Types of Ball Bearings {-} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: --- ## Ball Bearing Life Calculations {#bearing-life} The life of a rolling element bearing is inherently **statistical**—even identical bearings operating under identical conditions will fail at different times due to the random nature of material fatigue. Understanding this statistical behavior is essential for proper bearing selection and reliability engineering. ### Understanding Statistical Bearing Life {-} ::: {.callout-think} **Before You Read:** If you tested 100 identical bearings under identical loads and speeds, would they all fail at the same time? What factors might cause variation in their lifetimes? ::: When bearings fail, they do so by **fatigue spalling**—small flakes of material breaking away from the rolling surfaces due to repeated stress cycles. The location where a fatigue crack initiates depends on microscopic material imperfections (inclusions, voids, grain boundaries) that vary randomly from bearing to bearing, even in high-quality manufacturing. If we test a large group of identical bearings under identical conditions and plot the number of failures against operating time, we get a distribution of bearing lives. This distribution is **not** a normal (Gaussian) distribution—it follows a **Weibull distribution**, which is skewed to the right. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Statistical distribution of bearing failures showing L10, L50, and mean life concepts.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/bearing-life-distribution-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ### L10 vs. L50: Which Life Do We Use? {-} The figure above illustrates several important life values: | Life Designation | Definition | Typical Relationship | |:-----------------|:-----------|:---------------------| | **L10** | Life exceeded by 90% of bearings | **Design basis** (conservative) | | **L50** (median) | Life exceeded by 50% of bearings | L50 ≈ 5 × L10 | | **Mean life** | Average life of all bearings | Mean ≈ 5.4 × L10 | ::: {.callout-industry} **Why L10, not L50?** In most engineering applications, we design for the **L10 life** because: 1. **Safety margin:** 90% of bearings will exceed this life—conservative design 2. **Replacement planning:** We know when 10% might start failing 3. **Industry standard:** All bearing catalogs use L10 ratings (ISO 281) If we designed for L50 life, half of our bearings would fail before the "rated" life—unacceptable for most applications! ::: The relationship between L10 and L50 also explains an important insight: if a bearing achieves its L10 life, it still has substantial remaining life. The **median bearing** (L50) lasts about 5 times longer than L10! ### The L10 Life Concept {-} > **Definition:** The L10 life is the number of revolutions (or hours at a given speed) that **90% of a group of identical bearings** will complete or exceed before the first evidence of fatigue failure (flaking/spalling). In other words, 10% of bearings will fail before reaching L10 life, while 90% will survive. ### Basic Life Equation {-} The fundamental bearing life equation is: $$L_{10} = \left(\frac{C}{P}\right)^p \times 10^6 \text{ revolutions}$$ **Where:** | Symbol | Description | Units | |:-------|:------------|:------| | $L_{10}$ | Basic rating life | revolutions | | $C$ | Basic dynamic load rating | N or lbf | | $P$ | Equivalent dynamic bearing load | N or lbf | | $p$ | Life exponent | — | **Life Exponent Values:** - **Ball bearings:** $p = 3$ - **Roller bearings:** $p = 10/3 \approx 3.33$ ### Converting to Hours {-} For bearings operating at constant speed, it is more practical to express life in hours: $$L_{10h} = \frac{L_{10}}{60 \cdot n} = \frac{1}{60 \cdot n}\left(\frac{C}{P}\right)^p \times 10^6 \text{ hours}$$ Where $n$ is the rotational speed in RPM. This simplifies to: $$L_{10h} = \frac{10^6}{60 \cdot n}\left(\frac{C}{P}\right)^p$$ --- ### Equivalent Dynamic Load {-} When a bearing experiences both radial ($F_r$) and axial ($F_a$) loads simultaneously, an **equivalent dynamic load** ($P$) must be calculated: $$P = X \cdot F_r + Y \cdot F_a$$ **Where:** | Factor | Description | |:-------|:------------| | $X$ | Radial load factor (from bearing tables) | | $Y$ | Axial load factor (from bearing tables) | | $F_r$ | Applied radial load | | $F_a$ | Applied axial (thrust) load | For **pure radial loading** (most common case): $P = F_r$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-industry} **Design Insight:** If you can reduce the bearing load by just 20%, you nearly **double** the bearing life! Understanding this mechanism is essential for designing reliable bushing applications. ### The Wedge Effect {#sec-wedge-effect} When a shaft begins to rotate inside a lubricated bushing, something remarkable happens. The shaft doesn't rotate concentrically within the bore—instead, it shifts slightly off-center, creating a **converging wedge** of oil between the shaft and bearing surfaces. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The hydrodynamic wedge: shaft rotation drags oil into the converging gap, building pressure that lifts the shaft.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/fig-hydrodynamic-wedge-1.png){#fig-hydrodynamic-wedge fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: The physics of this process are elegant: 1. **Shaft rotation drags oil** into the narrowing gap (viscous drag) 2. **Oil cannot escape fast enough** through the narrow exit 3. **Pressure builds up** in the converging zone 4. **The pressure "pushes back"** against the shaft, lifting it 5. **At sufficient speed**, the shaft floats entirely on oil—no metal contact This is the **hydrodynamic cushion**: a self-generated oil film that supports the shaft load through fluid pressure alone. ### The Pressure Distribution {#sec-pressure-distribution} The pressure profile that develops in the oil film is not uniform. Maximum pressure occurs in the converging wedge region, just before the minimum film thickness point: $$ p = \frac{6 \mu U}{h^2} \frac{dh}{dx} $$ {#eq-reynolds-simplified} **Where:** | Symbol | Description | |:-------|:------------| | $p$ | Local pressure in the oil film | | $\mu$ | Dynamic viscosity of the lubricant | | $U$ | Surface velocity of the shaft | | $h$ | Local film thickness | | $dh/dx$ | Rate of change of film thickness | This is a simplified form of the **Reynolds equation**, which governs hydrodynamic lubrication. The key insight is that pressure only develops where the film is **converging** ($dh/dx < 0$)—in diverging regions, the pressure drops back to ambient. ::: {.callout-industry} **Industry Application:** Modern automotive engines rely entirely on hydrodynamic lubrication for their crankshaft main bearings and connecting rod bearings. At idle speed (~800 RPM), a typical crankshaft main bearing develops oil film pressures of 5-10 MPa, supporting loads of several kilonewtons on a film just 2-5 micrometers thick. At highway speeds, this film pressure can exceed 50 MPa. ::: ### Eccentricity Ratio {#sec-eccentricity} The position of the shaft within the bearing is characterized by the **eccentricity ratio** ($\varepsilon$): $$ \varepsilon = \frac{e}{c} $$ {#eq-eccentricity-ratio} **Where:** - $e$ = distance between bearing center and shaft center (eccentricity) - $c$ = radial clearance = $(D - d)/2$ (bearing bore radius minus shaft radius) | $\varepsilon$ Value | Meaning | |:--------------------|:--------| | 0 | Shaft is perfectly centered (no load, or very high speed) | | 0.3 - 0.7 | Normal operating range for hydrodynamic bearings | | → 1.0 | Shaft approaching contact with bearing (high load or low speed) | The minimum film thickness is directly related to eccentricity: $$ h_{min} = c(1 - \varepsilon) $$ {#eq-min-film-thickness} For safe operation, the minimum film thickness must exceed the combined surface roughness of the shaft and bearing, plus a safety margin for contaminants and vibration. Try it: the shaft sits lower in the bearing as the load goes up or the speed comes down. Drag the eccentricity ratio and watch the film thin out. The picture exaggerates the clearance so you can see it. ```{=html}

--- ## Oil Circulation in Sintered Bearings {#sec-oil-circulation} For sintered oil-impregnated bushings (see Chapter @sec-chap-sintering for manufacturing details), the hydrodynamic mechanism works in concert with the porous structure. The following diagram shows how oil circulates through a sintered bearing during operation: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Oil circulation mechanism in a sintered oil-impregnated bearing. The porous structure stores oil that is released during operation and recovered during rest periods.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/fig-oil-circulation-1.png){#fig-oil-circulation fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- ## The Stribeck Curve: Understanding Lubrication Regimes {#sec-stribeck-curve} The transition from metal-to-metal contact to full hydrodynamic separation doesn't happen instantly. German engineer Richard Stribeck (1861-1950) systematically studied this transition and developed one of the most important diagrams in tribology—the **Stribeck curve**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The Stribeck curve showing the three lubrication regimes as a function of the bearing parameter.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/fig-stribeck-curve-1.png){#fig-stribeck-curve fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ### The Three Lubrication Regimes {#sec-lubrication-regimes} The Stribeck curve reveals three distinct operating regimes, determined by the **bearing parameter** (also called the Hersey number or Sommerfeld variable): $$ \text{Bearing Parameter} = \frac{\mu N}{P} $$ {#eq-hersey-number} **Where:** | Symbol | Description | |:-------|:------------| | $\mu$ | Dynamic viscosity of the lubricant | | $N$ | Rotational speed (or sliding velocity) | | $P$ | Bearing pressure (load per unit projected area) | --- **1. Boundary Lubrication** (Low bearing parameter) At low speeds, high loads, or low viscosity, the oil film is too thin to separate the surfaces. The shaft and bearing make direct metal-to-metal contact at their surface asperities (microscopic peaks). - **Friction coefficient:** 0.08 - 0.15 (high) - **Wear:** Significant—asperities deform and break off - **Protection:** Depends on boundary additives in the oil (anti-wear, extreme pressure) - **Typical conditions:** Startup, shutdown, slow oscillating motion ::: {.callout-check} **Quick Check:** Why is startup the most damaging period for a hydrodynamic bearing? ::: --- **2. Mixed Lubrication** (Intermediate bearing parameter) As speed increases or load decreases, a partial fluid film develops. The load is shared between the oil film (hydrodynamic pressure) and the remaining asperity contacts. - **Friction coefficient:** 0.02 - 0.08 (decreasing rapidly) - **Wear:** Moderate—some contact remains - **Transition zone:** Most sensitive to operating conditions - **Typical conditions:** Acceleration/deceleration, variable loads --- **3. Hydrodynamic Lubrication** (High bearing parameter) At sufficient speed, the shaft "lifts off" completely and floats on the oil cushion. There is no metal-to-metal contact—all load is carried by fluid pressure. - **Friction coefficient:** 0.001 - 0.01 (very low) - **Wear:** Essentially zero (only contamination-related) - **Friction source:** Viscous shearing of the oil film - **Typical conditions:** Continuous rotation at design speed Notice that friction actually **increases** slightly at very high bearing parameters. This is because the viscous drag in the oil film increases with speed—but this "friction" doesn't cause wear since no contact occurs. --- ### Practical Implications for Bearing Design {#sec-stribeck-implications} The Stribeck curve has profound implications for bearing selection and design: | Design Goal | Implication | |:------------|:------------| | **Maximize bearing life** | Operate in the hydrodynamic regime; avoid boundary conditions | | **Minimum speed requirement** | Must exceed the transition speed for hydrodynamic lubrication | | **Oil selection** | Higher viscosity → lower bearing parameter → earlier transition to hydrodynamic | | **Clearance design** | Affects film thickness and transition point | | **Startup/shutdown wear** | Unavoidable boundary contact; limit start-stop cycles or use hydrostatic assist | ::: {.callout-industry} **Industry Application:** Large turbine bearings in power plants use **hydrostatic jacking**—externally pressurized oil is pumped into the bearing at startup to lift the shaft before rotation begins. This eliminates the boundary lubrication phase entirely, preventing wear during the 10-15 seconds it takes to reach hydrodynamic speed. ::: ### Watch It Happen: One Start–Stop Cycle {#sec-oil-film-cycle-video} The animation below follows a bushing through a complete start–stop cycle: at rest, startup, liftoff, full-speed running, coast-down, and touchdown. Four views update together. The bearing cross-section shows the shaft position and the oil-film pressure. The Stribeck curve marks where the bearing is operating. The zoom panel shows the asperities at $h_{min}$, and the last panel plots cumulative wear. ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} {{< video images/bearing-oil-film-cycle.mp4 title="Oil film formation in a plain bearing over one start-stop cycle" >}} ::: ::: {.content-visible unless-format="html"} ![One start–stop cycle of a plain bearing, shown during full-speed running. The animated version in the online edition steps through startup, liftoff, running, and shutdown.](images/bearing-oil-film-cycle-poster.png){#fig-oil-film-cycle fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: Watch for three things: - **Liftoff and touchdown happen at different speeds.** Oil that has warmed up during running is thinner (lower viscosity) than the cold oil at startup. So on the way down, the bearing parameter drops below the transition value at a *higher* speed than liftoff happened on the way up. (The animation writes viscosity as η, as in the Stribeck curve figure above, and uses μ for the friction coefficient.) - **The shaft centre does not move straight up.** It swings off to the side of the load line as the wedge forms. That is why $h_{min}$ sits downstream of the bottom of the bore. - **Almost all of the wear happens in the first and last few seconds.** Once $h_{min}$ is about three times the combined surface roughness, the wear curve goes flat. A bushing's life therefore depends mostly on how many start–stop cycles it sees, not on how many hours it runs. The model behind the animation is simplified for teaching. It uses the short-bearing (Ocvirk) pressure and attitude-angle relations, a lagged film-thickness response, and Archard-type wear proportional to asperity load × sliding speed. The trends are right, but the numbers are illustrative only. For sintered self-lubricating bearings (see Chapter @sec-chap-sintering), the oil stored in the porous structure is released by heat and pumping action during operation. However, at very low speeds or oscillating motion, hydrodynamic films cannot develop—this is why **graphite-impregnated sintered bearings** are used instead for such applications, providing solid lubrication rather than relying on fluid film formation. --- ## How the Oil Circulates, Step by Step {#sec-oil-circulation-diagram} The oil-circulation figure earlier in this chapter (@fig-oil-circulation) shows one instant of the process. The porous structure is an oil reservoir that keeps refilling the hydrodynamic film, and the cycle runs in a loop: 1. **At rest**, the pores are full and a thin oil layer coats the bore. 2. **At start-up**, friction warms the bearing. The oil expands and thins, and flows out of the pores into the clearance. 3. **As the shaft turns**, it drags oil into the converging wedge, pressure builds, and the shaft lifts onto the film. 4. **While running**, the high-pressure zone pushes oil back into the pores, and the low-pressure zone on the other side lets oil flow out of them. The oil circulates through the wall. 5. **At shutdown**, the bearing cools, and capillary action pulls the oil back into the pores to wait for the next start. ## Try it yourself: put the circulation cycle in order {#sec-tryit-oil-cycle} The steps are shuffled. Move each one up or down until the cycle runs from rest to the next rest. ```{=html}
``` --- ## PV Limits for Bushings {#pv-limits} The **PV limit** is the most important design criterion for plain bearings. It represents the maximum combination of **bearing pressure** (P) and **sliding velocity** (V) that the bearing material can sustain without excessive wear or failure. ### The PV Concept {-} $$PV = P \times V$$ **Where:** | Symbol | Description | Typical Units | |:-------|:------------|:--------------| | $P$ | Bearing pressure | psi (or MPa) | | $V$ | Sliding velocity | ft/min (or m/s) | | $PV$ | PV factor | psi·ft/min (or MPa·m/s) | ### Calculating Bearing Pressure (P) {-} For a journal bearing (shaft in a bushing): $$P = \frac{F}{d \times L}$$ **Where:** | Symbol | Description | |:-------|:------------| | $F$ | Radial load on the bearing (lbf or N) | | $d$ | Shaft (journal) diameter (in or mm) | | $L$ | Bearing length (in or mm) | > **Note:** This is the **projected area** method, using $A = d \times L$, not the cylindrical surface area. ### Calculating Sliding Velocity (V) {-} $$V = \pi \times d \times n$$ For consistent units: **English:** $$V = \frac{\pi \times d \times n}{12} \quad \text{(ft/min, where } d \text{ in inches, } n \text{ in RPM)}$$ **Metric:** $$V = \frac{\pi \times d \times n}{60,000} \quad \text{(m/s, where } d \text{ in mm, } n \text{ in RPM)}$$ --- ### PV Limit Visualization {-} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![PV limit diagram showing safe operating region for different bushing materials.](02-03-Bearings_files/figure-html/pv-limit-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: --- ### Design Rules for PV {-} 1. **Calculate the actual PV** for your application 2. **Select a bushing material** with a PV limit **at least 2× higher** than calculated 3. **Check individual P and V limits** separately (materials have maximums for each) 4. **Consider temperature effects**—PV limits decrease at elevated temperatures ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

## Bearing vs. Bushing Selection Guide {#sec-selection-guide} When should you use a ball bearing versus a bushing? The choice depends on operating conditions, space constraints, and maintenance requirements. For bushings, the decision between oil-impregnated and solid-lubricant types depends on the motion profile and environment—continuous rotation favors oil-impregnated bearings that can develop hydrodynamic films, while oscillating or high-temperature applications favor graphite-impregnated designs (see Chapter @sec-chap-sintering for details on manufacturing both types).
